<explanation>
Based on the project’s file tree and README, this is Kanboard – a PHP-based project management application that adheres to the Kanban methodology. Although it’s now in maintenance mode, its architecture remains representative of a robust, full-stack web application that follows an MVC-like structure with dedicated modules for actions, controllers, models, core functions, APIs, and plugins.

Below is a guideline on how to draw an accurate and detailed system design/architecture diagram for Kanboard:

1. Identify and Isolate the Main Components:
   • Frontend & User Interface:
     - The UI is built using view templates found in the “app/Template” directory.
     - Assets (CSS, JavaScript, images, and fonts in “assets/”) support the presentation.
     - Entry points like “index.php” or “jsonrpc.php” receive incoming HTTP requests.

   • Controllers and HTTP Layer:
     - Controllers in “app/Controller” receive HTTP requests, process the user’s actions, and select the proper views.
     - Middleware fundamentals (present in “app/Middleware” and “app/Api/Middleware”) provide authentication, authorization, and request routing.

   • Business Logic and Actions:
     - “app/Action” encapsulates the business rules and actions that can be triggered throughout the application.
     - The “app/Api” section contains APIs that expose various actions and procedures to external consumers.

   • Data Handling and Models:
     - “app/Model” contains data models that represent domains like tasks, projects, users, and notifications.
     - This layer communicates with storage (the actual database, configured via “config.default.php” and supported by “libs/picodb”).

   • Core Framework Services:
     - “app/Core” houses integral classes for caching, event management, HTTP handling, logging, security, LDAP, and session management.
     - It also includes utility classes for template parsing, object storage, and plugin management.

   • External Libraries and Third-Party Integration:
     - The “libs” folder contains many external libraries (e.g., SwiftMailer for mailing, JSON-RPC, Captcha, etc.) that support various functionalities.
     - The “plugins” directory allows for extensibility by custom modules.

   • Configuration, Deployment, and DevOps:
     - Top-level configuration files (e.g., “Dockerfile”, “docker-compose.yml”, Vagrantfile, Makefile) indicate containerization and deployment scripts.
     - Files under “.github”, “docker”, and “.devcontainer” manage CI/CD and developer tooling.
     - Testing is organized under the “tests” directory for integration and unit tests.

2. Depict the Relationships and Data Flow:
   • Represent the HTTP layer (entry points) routing requests to the controllers.
   • Illustrate controllers calling business logic – invoking “actions” and “procedures” (in “app/Action” and “app/Api/Procedure”).
   • Show models handling database operations connected to business logic.
   • Map out the events and notifications where triggered actions result in background jobs (queues in “app/Job” and event dispatching in “app/Event” and “app/EventBuilder”).
   • Include arrows to indicate data flow from the UI to controllers, then business logic, and then models/data storage.
   • Show integration with external libraries (e.g., mailing through SwiftMailer, external task handling under “app/Core/ExternalTask”, or JSON-RPC APIs).

3. Note Architectural Patterns and Design Principles:
   • MVC/Layered Architecture:
     - Emphasize the separation between user interface (templates/assets), controllers & middleware, and the model/data layers.
   • Plugin/Extension Architecture:
     - Highlight the “app/Core/Plugin” module and the “plugins” directory where plugins can intercept logic via hooks.
   • Dependency Injection & Service Providers:
     - Note the “app/ServiceProvider” directory that sets up services for actions, authentication, logging, etc.
   • Modularization:
     - The system is split into discrete modules (Actions, API, Auth, Model, Core, etc.), each with well-defined responsibilities.

4. Guidelines for Tailoring the Diagram:
   • Use distinct colors and shapes:
     - Represent UI components (templates, assets) with one color.
     - Controllers and Middleware with another; business logic/actions in a separate block.
     - Models and persistence layers should have their own distinctive icon.
   • Label each component clearly.
   • Use directional arrows to show data flow:
     - For example, from “index.php” (or the HTTP entry point) → Controller → Action (business logic) → Model → Database.
   • Include external integrations:
     - PHP libraries and external services (like email, API gateways) should be represented as connectors.
   • Depict deployment environment components:
     - Show containerization with Docker (using “docker-compose.yml”, “Dockerfile”) and possible CI/CD pipelines from “.github/workflows”.

5. Suggested Diagram Layout:
   • At the top, show the Client/Browser initiating HTTP requests.
   • Next layer: Web Server (with entry points like “index.php” and “jsonrpc.php”).
   • The application layer:
       - UI Layer: Templates and assets.
       - Controller Layer: Routing to controllers.
       - Business Logic Layer: Actions and API procedures.
       - Data Access Layer: Models (using libraries like PicoDb) connecting to the Database.
       - Core services: Middleware (authentication, authorization), caching, event dispatcher.
   • On the side or as adjunct components, include external libraries/services and plugin mechanisms.
   • At the bottom, include DevOps-related items (Docker, Vagrant, automated tests).

6. Final Tips:
   • Be very detailed when mapping out sub-components like “app/Core” (which itself includes modules for HTTP, LDAP, cache, etc.).
   • Use labels that reflect the actual directory structure so that someone reviewing the diagram can easily locate the implementation.
   • Ensure that the data flow (request/response cycle) and control flow (event-driven messaging via the event dispatcher and job queue) are clearly marked.

By following these guidelines and mapping out each physical module along with their interactions, your system design diagram will provide a comprehensive, accurate depiction of Kanboard’s architecture – from the entry point through business logic to the data storage and external integrations.
</explanation>
